faq.title: Answers in three lines
faq.intro: The questions that come up most often before a first analysis.

start.question: How long before my first analysis?
start.answer: Twenty-four hours after you draw a field outline. History usually goes back three to five years of satellite archives, so you can compare the current season with previous ones from day one.

accuracy.question: How accurate is a satellite analysis?
accuracy.answer: Sentinel-2 delivers a 10-metre pixel, meaning one measurement point every 100 m². That is enough to zone a field and locate a hotspot, not to diagnose a single tree — that is what the drone is for.

clouds.question: What happens when it is cloudy?
clouds.answer: Covered pixels are masked automatically and excluded from the calculation. Cloud cover is displayed for each pass; in the Mediterranean, over 80 % of dry-season passes are usable.

size.question: Is there a minimum area?
size.answer: No, monitoring works from one hectare. Below that the pixel count becomes too low for reliable zoning, but the vigour curve remains usable.

data.question: Who owns my data?
data.answer: You do. Outlines, readings and history remain your property: they are never sold or passed to third parties, and you can export them or request deletion at any time.

whatIs.question: What is RoboCare?
whatIs.answer: RoboCare is a Tunisian AgriTech company that helps farmers monitor their crops using satellite imagery, artificial intelligence, and agricultural IoT sensors. Founded in Sfax in 2021, RoboCare turns satellite and sensor data into clear, field-level decisions — irrigation timing, nitrogen needs, early disease detection — for olive groves, cereals, citrus, and greenhouse crops. No hardware is required to start: a satellite-based analysis is available within 24 hours of adding a field.

howHelps.question: How does RoboCare help farmers?
howHelps.answer: RoboCare replaces guesswork with field-level evidence. Satellite and drone imagery reveal exactly which zones of a field are under water or nutrient stress, IoT soil sensors confirm what’s happening below ground, and AI models turn both into concrete actions — where to irrigate first, where to apply nitrogen, which trees need attention. Farmers act on real conditions instead of walking the whole field or waiting for visible symptoms.

whyChoose.question: Why choose RoboCare for precision agriculture?
whyChoose.answer: RoboCare’s models are trained on Mediterranean growing conditions, not imported from another climate, and retrained every season. The team is based in Sfax, working alongside the farms it monitors rather than remotely. Coverage already spans over 100,000 hectares across olive, cereal, citrus, and greenhouse operations, with satellite monitoring, IoT sensors, and agricultural drones combined in a single platform — and no hardware required to get started.

concepts.title: What happens between the satellite and your field
concepts.lead: Before choosing a solution, it helps to understand what it rests on. Here are the six agronomic and technical building blocks behind every RoboCare recommendation.

precision.title: Precision agriculture
precision.text: Precision agriculture starts from a simple observation: a field is never uniform. Soil depth changes, available water capacity varies by tens of millimetres from one end to the other, and a single rate applied everywhere is necessarily excessive somewhere and insufficient elsewhere.
precision.text2: Managing with precision means splitting the field into coherent zones and treating each according to its real need. Remote sensing makes that possible without probing the soil every twenty metres: the canopy’s spectral response already integrates the combined effect of soil, water and nutrition.
points: Within-field zoning derived from spectral response
Variable rates instead of uniform ones
Season-to-season comparison on the same grid

satellite.title: Satellite imagery and remote sensing
satellite.text: The Copernicus programme’s Sentinel-2 satellites pass over Tunisia every five days and measure the light reflected by the canopy across thirteen spectral bands, from blue to shortwave infrared. A healthy plant absorbs red for photosynthesis and reflects near infrared heavily; a stressed plant does the opposite, progressively.
satellite.text2: That imbalance becomes measurable long before it turns into visible yellowing. This is the whole value of remote sensing: it gives access to a physiological signal, not merely a photograph of the field.
points: Five-day revisit, archives available since 2015
Thirteen spectral bands, three of them in the red edge
Automated atmospheric correction and cloud masking

iot.title: Ground IoT sensors
iot.text: Satellites observe the canopy; they cannot see what happens forty centimetres down. IoT stations fill that blind spot: staged moisture probes, soil temperature, electrical conductivity and, depending on the site, a rain gauge and anemometer, all sampled every fifteen minutes.
iot.text2: Transmitted over LoRaWAN — several kilometres of range at a power draw that allows years of autonomy on battery and solar panel — these readings calibrate the satellite model’s thresholds against the farm’s actual soil conditions.
points: Moisture measured at several root depths
LoRaWAN or 4G depending on site coverage
Solar powered, annual maintenance

drone.title: Multispectral drones
drone.text: When the question drops to the scale of a tree or a row, ten-metre resolution is no longer enough. The drone carries a multispectral and a thermal camera and flies a few dozen metres up: each pixel then covers two to five centimetres of ground.
drone.text2: At that resolution you count trees one by one, spot a blocked emitter by its thermal signature and map a disease outbreak to the metre. Flights are planned in advance and the report is generated automatically after processing.
points: Centimetre resolution, tree-by-tree health
Thermal imaging to check irrigation uniformity
Planned missions, automatic orthomosaic and report

ai.title: Applied artificial intelligence
ai.text: A raw vegetation index is noisy: sun angle, surface moisture, phenological stage and soil type all shift it without any agronomic problem being involved. The models’ job is precisely to separate that noise from the useful signal.
ai.text2: We combine segmentation networks to outline abnormal zones, time-series models to detect a break in trend, and classifiers trained on field photographs to propose a disease hypothesis. Every prediction is checked against the agronomist’s observations, and models are retrained at the end of each season.
points: Image segmentation to isolate stress zones
Break detection on the field’s time series
Field feedback loop and seasonal retraining

irrigation.title: Smart irrigation
irrigation.text: Managing irrigation is not about watering more, but about knowing which sector has actually depleted its reserve. The water balance combines reference evapotranspiration, the crop coefficient for the current stage, effective rainfall and probe moisture readings.
irrigation.text2: The output is a volume per sector and per watering round, revised at every satellite pass. On olive, it supports controlled deficit irrigation: deliberately reducing supply during less sensitive phases without compromising fruit set.
points: Water balance per sector, revised at every pass
Detection of drip-network unevenness
Managed deficit irrigation on perennial crops

faq.title: Arboriculture and large-scale crops
faq.intro: What RoboCare changes in practice, orchard by orchard and field by field.

monitorOliveOrchards.question: Can RoboCare monitor olive orchards?
monitorOliveOrchards.answer: Yes — olive monitoring is one of RoboCare’s core solutions, Olive Care. It tracks tree-by-tree vigor using satellite and drone imagery, flags missing or declining trees, monitors water stress ahead of flowering and fruit set, and screens for early signs of peacock spot disease. Farms using it have reduced irrigation water use by around 28% while managing the tree’s natural alternate-bearing cycle more predictably.

oliveProductionImprove.question: How can precision agriculture improve olive production?
oliveProductionImprove.answer: Olive trees tolerate drought but pay for it the following year through reduced yield — the alternate-bearing effect. By tracking vigor and water stress tree-by-tree before flowering, RoboCare lets growers time deficit irrigation precisely, keeping trees under just enough stress to manage vegetative growth without triggering a yield crash the next season. Early peacock spot detection also means treatment goes only where disease pressure is confirmed.

fruitTreeStress.question: Can RoboCare detect stress in fruit trees?
fruitTreeStress.answer: Yes. Beyond olives, RoboCare’s Citrus Care solution applies the same tree-level monitoring to citrus orchards — combining satellite indices with drone imagery when finer detail is needed to spot water or nutrient stress in individual trees before it’s visible on the ground. The same approach extends to other fruit tree crops as farms bring new orchards onto the platform.

suitableLargeFarms.question: Is RoboCare suitable for large farms?
suitableLargeFarms.answer: Yes — RoboCare already monitors over 100,000 hectares, and pricing scales with a degressive tier beyond 100 hectares plus a specific rate for cooperatives grouping several members. Cereal Care, for example, turns NDRE readings into nitrogen modulation maps across large blocks, tracks emergence and lodging, and estimates yield by zone weeks before harvest — built for scale, not just single small plots.

irrigationFertilizationLargeFarms.question: How can large-scale farms optimize irrigation and fertilization with RoboCare?
irrigationFertilizationLargeFarms.answer: Across a large farm, RoboCare’s platform zones every field automatically from satellite indices, so irrigation and nitrogen decisions are made per homogeneous zone instead of per whole field. NDWI flags where water stress starts first, NDRE drives variable-rate nitrogen maps, and the same maps export directly to the formats most spreading consoles already accept.

multiplePlotsMonitoring.question: Can RoboCare monitor multiple agricultural plots?
multiplePlotsMonitoring.answer: Yes — the platform is built around managing a full portfolio of fields from one dashboard, not a single plot. Each field keeps its own history, indices, and alerts, while the dashboard surfaces which fields need attention across the whole operation at a glance. This is exactly the use case cooperatives rely on, since it lets one account track many members’ plots under a single, consistent view.

architecture.title: How the platform is built
architecture.lead: Five layers, from downloading a raw image to the notification landing on a phone.

ingestion.title: Ingestion
ingestion.text: Scheduled retrieval of Sentinel-2 and Landsat scenes, collection of sensor frames through the LoRaWAN gateway and the 4G network, import of drone flights and local weather data.

processing.title: Processing
processing.text: Atmospheric correction, masking of clouds and their shadows, clipping per field, index computation and inference model execution across parallelised jobs.

storage.title: Storage
storage.text: Rasters kept in a cloud-optimised format so only the requested window is read, geometries and time series in a spatial database, cold archives for multi-year history.

api.title: API layer
api.text: A documented REST API exposes fields, indices, alerts and reports. It serves the web interface, the mobile app and third-party integrations through the same authentication.

delivery.title: Delivery
delivery.text: Vector maps rendered in the browser, PDF reports generated on demand, notifications routed to email, SMS or WhatsApp according to each user’s preference.

encryption.title: Encryption

ownership.title: Data ownership

availability.title: Availability and synchronisation

indices.title: Four indices, four different questions
indices.lead: An index is not a health score: it is a ratio between two spectral bands, sensitive to one specific phenomenon. Using the right one at the right stage avoids most misreadings.

ndvi.name: NDVI
ndvi.useFor: Season tracking, broad zoning, spotting a drop. Saturates when the canopy is very dense.

ndre.name: NDRE
ndre.measures: Chlorophyll content, hence canopy nitrogen status.
ndre.useFor: Variable-rate nitrogen on cereals and dense canopies, where NDVI no longer discriminates.

ndwi.name: NDWI
ndwi.measures: Water content of leaves and canopy.
ndwi.useFor: Early water stress detection, before vigour visibly drops.

savi.name: SAVI
savi.useFor: Row-planted perennials and early growth stages, when soil fills much of the pixel.

indices.note: All four indices are computed at every pass and kept in the field’s history.

stack.title: The technical chain, block by block
stack.lead: What the words “AI”, “big data” and “GIS” actually cover inside the RoboCare platform.

vision.title: Disease detection and tree counting
vision.text: Convolutional networks segment the drone orthomosaic to isolate each canopy, then classify its condition. On olive groves this counts the trees, identifies empty planting spots and flags crowns whose signature suggests peacock spot. A disease hypothesis always comes with a confidence level, never as a closed diagnosis.

ml.title: Forecasting and break-detection models
ml.text: Time-series models learn the normal trajectory of a field for a given crop-climate pair and flag deviations that fall outside the expected interval. Yield models, trained on histories declared by partner farms, produce a per-zone estimate several weeks before harvest.

bigdata.title: Processing a million images
bigdata.text: A Sentinel-2 scene weighs several hundred megabytes and covers 110 km across. Processing is split into parallel tasks, rasters are stored in a cloud-optimised format so only the useful window is read, and indices are pre-computed so opening a field stays instant.

api.title: A documented REST API
api.text: Fields, indices, alerts and reports are available through an authenticated REST API with pagination and webhooks. Cooperatives use it to feed their own management systems; equipment makers, to pull a variable-rate map their spreader console can read.

gis.title: Geomatics and coordinate systems
gis.text: Imported outlines are reprojected automatically to a shared reference system, with local projection handling and topological validation. Variable-rate maps are exported in the formats expected by on-board consoles and RTK GPS receivers.

protocols.title: Field communication
protocols.text: LoRaWAN for remote sensors — kilometres of range at minimal power draw — 4G where coverage allows and throughput is needed, MQTT to push frames to the ingestion gateway, and local storage on the station whenever the network drops.

faq.title: Understanding the technology
faq.intro: What satellite monitoring, AI, and agricultural drones actually cover at RoboCare.

whatIsPrecisionAg.question: What is precision agriculture?
whatIsPrecisionAg.answer: Precision agriculture manages a field zone by zone instead of treating it as one uniform block — because soil, water, and vigor rarely are. It combines satellite and drone imagery, IoT soil sensors, and AI analysis to map exactly where a crop needs water, nitrogen, or attention, and where it doesn’t. The result is targeted action instead of blanket treatment: inputs go where they’re useful, not everywhere at once.

satelliteImproveFarming.question: How does satellite monitoring improve farming?
satelliteImproveFarming.answer: Satellite monitoring gives farmers a view of the entire field every few days, without walking it. RoboCare processes Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery automatically at each pass, masking clouds and calculating vegetation indices like NDVI and NDRE to reveal vigor changes before they’re visible to the eye. Three to five years of archived imagery let farmers compare the current season against past ones from day one.

detectStressEarly.question: How can farmers detect crop stress early?
detectStressEarly.answer: The earliest signs of water or nutrient stress show up in the near-infrared spectrum before leaves visibly wilt or yellow. RoboCare’s NDWI index flags water stress specifically, ahead of a visible drop in vigor, while NDRE tracks chlorophyll and nitrogen status in dense canopies where NDVI saturates. Combined with IoT soil moisture probes, this gives an early warning days to weeks before symptoms are visible on the ground.

analyzeSatelliteImages.question: How does RoboCare analyze satellite images?
analyzeSatelliteImages.answer: Every satellite pass is processed automatically: cloud-covered pixels are masked out, and the remaining imagery is converted into vegetation indices — NDVI, NDRE, NDWI, and SAVI — at 10-meter resolution from Sentinel-2. Each index is stored in the field’s history, so a farmer sees not just today’s snapshot but a trend line across the season and against previous years, with zones of concern highlighted automatically.

ndviNdreExplained.question: What are NDVI and NDRE indices?
ndviNdreExplained.answer: NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) measures overall vegetation density and vigor from near-infrared and red light — useful for season-long tracking and zoning, though it saturates in very dense canopies. NDRE (Normalized Difference Red Edge) reads chlorophyll and nitrogen status instead, using the red-edge band, and stays accurate exactly where NDVI stops discriminating — making it the index RoboCare uses for nitrogen modulation on cereals.

aiDecisionMaking.question: How does AI help agricultural decision-making?
aiDecisionMaking.answer: RoboCare’s AI models are trained on Mediterranean time series, not imported from another climate, and retrained every season. They handle three tasks: image segmentation to delimit stressed zones within a field, yield forecasting per crop, and disease classification from field photos. Instead of raw index values, a farmer receives a direct recommendation — irrigate this zone, treat that one — reducing analysis to a decision.

droneInspection.question: Does RoboCare provide drone inspection services?
droneInspection.answer: Yes. RoboCare’s agricultural drones carry multispectral and thermal sensors for centimeter-resolution inspection — the level of detail satellite imagery can’t reach. Missions are programmed and flown over a field or orchard, and results are compiled automatically into a report per zone, including individual tree counts where relevant. Drone inspection complements satellite monitoring rather than replacing it: satellite for the whole season, drone when a closer look is needed.

droneDetectProblems.question: How can drones detect crop problems?
droneDetectProblems.answer: Flying much closer to the canopy than a satellite, RoboCare’s drones capture centimeter-resolution multispectral and thermal imagery that reveals individual trees or plants under stress — not just a general zone. Thermal sensors pick up canopy temperature differences linked to water stress before wilting is visible, while multispectral bands support the same vegetation indices used at satellite scale, at a resolution fine enough to isolate a single affected tree.

droneFertilizationSpraying.question: Does RoboCare use drones for fertilization and spraying?
droneFertilizationSpraying.answer: RoboCare’s drone missions map exactly which zones of a field need nitrogen or treatment, based on NDRE and thermal readings — and that map can guide targeted, variable-rate fertilization and spraying instead of a uniform pass over the whole field. Inputs go only where the data shows they’re needed, which is the same principle behind RoboCare’s satellite-based nitrogen modulation on cereals, applied at drone resolution.

droneAdvantages.question: What are the advantages of drone-based agricultural treatments?
droneAdvantages.answer: Drone-based treatment targets exactly the zones that need it, based on a real map rather than a uniform application — reducing the volume of fertilizer or crop-protection product used, and its cost, without under-treating the areas that actually need it. Missions are programmed and flown quickly over a field or orchard, faster than manual scouting, and the resulting maps stay in RoboCare’s platform for the next season’s comparison.

approach.title: How we work
approach.lead: A method unchanged since 2021: start from an agronomic question, validate it in the field, and only industrialise what has held up for two seasons.

approach.title: Our approach
approach.text: We never start from an available technology and look for a use for it. We start from a decision the farmer has to make this week — irrigate or wait, split the dose or not — and work back to the data able to answer it. Many attractive ideas do not survive that filter.

method.title: Our methodology
method.text: Four stages: agronomic framing with the farmer, a prototype on a sample of fields, confrontation with ground readings over a full season, then production release with a calibrated threshold. A model that has not faced the field does not leave the lab.

expertise.title: Our expertise
expertise.text: Remote sensing and multispectral image processing, machine learning on time series, low-power embedded electronics, and Mediterranean agronomy — olive growing, rain-fed field crops, citrus irrigated under saline constraint.

innovation.title: Our innovation
innovation.text: Our own contribution lies less in generic algorithms than in their local calibration: stress thresholds adapted to carbonate soils, indices corrected for row canopies, and models retrained each season with partner agronomists’ observations.

local.title: A team on site
local.text: Based in Sfax, among the farms it monitors — not four flight hours from the nearest olive tree.

agronomy.title: Agronomy decides
agronomy.text: Every threshold in the platform was discussed with an agronomist before being coded, and corrected after field confrontation.

languages.title: In your language
languages.text: Interface, reports and alerts in French, English and Arabic, with no degraded version for any of the three.

noLockIn.title: No hardware lock-in
noLockIn.text: Satellite is enough to start. You only buy sensors if your fields draw a demonstrated benefit from them.

measurable.title: Verifiable results
measurable.text: Every figure we publish comes from an identified farm, compared with its own baseline before monitoring.

commitment.title: Our commitment
commitment.text: We commit to three things, and accept being judged on them: a reply to any request within 48 working hours; no resale and no sharing of your data with third parties, under any circumstances; and honesty about the limits of our models. When a prediction is uncertain, the platform says so. An alert presented as certain that turns out to be wrong costs far more, in trust, than ten acknowledged uncertainties.

stories.title: Three farms, three problems, three results

olive-farm-tunisia.title: 220 ha olive grove, Sfax
olive-farm-tunisia.challenge: Highly uneven yields from one block to the next with no clear explanation, and an irrigation bill up 18% over two seasons.
olive-farm-tunisia.solution: Full mapping of the estate, weekly NDVI monitoring, six soil moisture stations in the most heterogeneous sectors and a deficit irrigation schedule recalculated every week.
results: 28% of irrigation water saved over the season
Two peacock spot outbreaks treated before spreading

cereal-cooperative-beja.title: Cereal cooperative, Béja
cereal-cooperative-beja.meta: Durum wheat · 1,400 hectares · 38 members · Béja, Tunisia
cereal-cooperative-beja.challenge: Uniform nitrogen applications across all fields, with no visibility on which zones were genuinely deficient or on the yield expected before harvest.
cereal-cooperative-beja.solution: Variable-rate nitrogen maps generated from NDRE at tillering, distributed to members over WhatsApp, and per-field yield estimates a month before harvest.
results: Harvest planning brought forward by three weeks
38 farms on a single shared map

citrus-orchard-nabeul.title: 85 ha citrus orchard, Nabeul
citrus-orchard-nabeul.challenge: Progressive salinisation of the water table and unexplained yellowing on border rows, with fruit size losses recorded two seasons running.
citrus-orchard-nabeul.solution: Weekly NDVI and NDRE monitoring cross-referenced with eight conductivity probes, orchard zoning into four irrigation sectors, and targeted leaching only where salinity exceeded the threshold.
results: 21% of irrigation water saved over the season
Salinity brought back below threshold in three sectors out of four
Average fruit size back to 2022 levels

environment.title: What the farm gives back to its environment
environment.lead: In the Mediterranean, the limiting resource is not land, it is water. Every cubic metre saved on a field is a cubic metre left in the aquifer, and every sprayer pass avoided is fuel, time and chemical pressure removed.
environment.lead2: The figures below are averages recorded on farms monitored for at least two seasons, compared with their own baseline before monitoring.

aquifers.title: Protecting aquifers
aquifers.text: Tunisia’s coastal aquifers turn saline when abstraction outpaces recharge. Reducing pumped volumes without losing yield is the only sustainable path, and it is measurable meter in hand.

soil.title: Sparing the soil
soil.text: Fewer machinery passes means less compaction, and therefore better infiltration the following winter. Adjusted fertilisation also limits the excess nitrate that leaches below the root zone.

climate.title: Adapting to the climate
climate.text: Intervention windows shift from one year to the next. A field’s multi-year history gives an objective basis for adjusting dates rather than repeating last year’s calendar.

certification.title: Documenting sustainability
certification.text: Every recommended dose and every recorded intervention stays time-stamped. Buyers and certification bodies ask for that traceability: it exports straight from the platform, with no re-keying.

faq.title: Before you write to us
faq.intro: Answers to the questions we are asked most often on first contact.

hardware.question: Do I need to buy hardware to get started?
hardware.answer: No. The satellite is enough: you create an account, add a field, and the first analysis arrives within 24 hours. IoT sensors and drone flights come later, and only if your farm needs them.

delay.question: How quickly do you reply?
delay.answer: 48 working hours at most. For support on an existing account, go through the platform: those requests are prioritised.

languages.question: Which languages can we work in?
languages.answer: French, English and Arabic — in writing and on the phone. Platform alerts follow the same rule.

coverage.question: Do you work outside Tunisia?
coverage.answer: Tunisia remains our main market — RoboCare was founded here and the team is based in Sfax. The platform has recently expanded into Algeria in response to demand from several farms there. Satellite monitoring is available as soon as an account is created; IoT sensors and drone flights depend on local logistics coverage.

pricing.question: How is pricing calculated?
pricing.answer: By monitored area, with a decreasing tier above one hundred hectares and specific pricing for cooperatives grouping several members. Satellite monitoring is included; sensors and drone flights are billed separately, only if you install them.

integration.question: Can RoboCare connect to our existing tools?
integration.answer: Yes. A documented REST API exposes fields, indices, alerts and reports, and variable-rate maps export in the formats most spreader consoles expect. Describe your current system and we will tell you what is already supported.

security.question: Where is our data hosted?
security.answer: In ISO 27001 certified European data centres, with encryption in transit and at rest and daily backups. Your data is never sold or shared, and a full export or deletion is available on request.

tunisiaBase.question: Is RoboCare available in Tunisia?
tunisiaBase.answer: Yes — Tunisia is RoboCare’s home market. The company was founded in Sfax in 2021 and the platform already covers over 100,000 hectares nationwide, across olive groves, cereal farms, citrus orchards, and greenhouses. Support, onboarding, and the agronomist team are all based locally, so questions get answered by people familiar with Tunisian growing conditions, not a remote call center.

regionalFit.question: Are RoboCare’s solutions adapted to North African agriculture?
regionalFit.answer: Yes. RoboCare’s AI models are trained specifically on Mediterranean and North African growing conditions — the same dry-farming olive groves, irrigated cereals, and citrus orchards found across Tunisia and Algeria — rather than adapted from models built for European or American agriculture. Vegetation indices, irrigation thresholds, and disease alerts are calibrated to local climate and crop calendars, and retrained every season.
